title: COVID-19 symptoms, taste loss, and Alzheimer's-related brain mechanisms
summary: This community links COVID-19 to symptoms and taste or smell dysfunction in one healthcare-worker cohort (P1) and to brain microvascular injury, neuroinflammation, and Alzheimer's-related biomarkers in a network medicine study (P2). In P1, positive-test participants had temporarily more cough, headache, sore throat, muscle pain, and fever, with no increases after 30 days, and taste and smell dysfunction was associated with a positive test across all 90 days. P1 also reports no association found for several of these same symptoms, such as fever and headache, so its claims are mixed for those symptoms. P2 reports associations between COVID-19 and neuroinflammation, microvascular injury, and Alzheimer's biomarkers, and press coverage overstated its Alzheimer's link. Across the community, press coverage aligned with the paper for seven of the eight matched claims, with one overstatement.
key_findings:
- In P1, positive-test participants were associated with temporarily higher cough, headache, sore throat, muscle pain, and fever, with no increases seen after 30 days. ['60eeab60590fb6c4', '9c1dfb2b6de80c9f', '9ea394b324a292eb', 'c6d2274ff9fd422b', '1b30b042a7a377b5']
- In P1, COVID-19 positivity was associated with reduced taste and smell in about 30% of positive-test participants during all 90 days. ['6a21b16128ae8e45']
- In P1, COVID-19 positivity was associated with dyspnea that declined over time but never reached the level seen in negative-test participants. ['11fa44fe675aa575']
- In P1, no association found was reported for fever, headache, cough, sore throat, or muscle pain in some claims, conflicting with the temporary increases for the same symptoms. ['1c3068c2481398ea', '774d92a88ac5f8a1', '818c117b6a2c2cac', 'e47ade336ed4e24a', '3861a7586ffc161b']
- In P2, COVID-19 was associated with neuroinflammation, brain microvascular injury, and aberrant Alzheimer's biomarker expression, though press coverage overstated the Alzheimer's link. ['026bb4d33e942dd3', 'fe74e054721cb905', 'c0a14467886af68a', '8412c8190a66bd1f']

title: Long COVID associations with hypertension, dyspnoea, ventilation, age and sex
summary: This community covers long COVID (post-COVID syndrome) as the outcome, with hypertension, dyspnoea and mechanical ventilation as linked features, and age and female sex as exposures. Both papers report associations at strength 1 ('associated with'), with no causal wording and no null findings. The five claims all point in the direction of increase, so the papers do not conflict. The Swedish cohort reports hypertension as associated with the post-COVID syndrome cohort, though most of those individuals received that diagnosis before COVID-19. Press coverage was aligned with the paper for the three claims that had a matched press statement, and the other two claims had no matched press statement.
key_findings:
- Post-COVID syndrome cohorts were associated with higher rates of hypertension and dyspnoea than COVID-19-negative and COVID-19-positive controls. ['0979f5e8f25bbe69', '7a5991d31d273132']
- Mechanical ventilation during initial COVID-19 was associated with post-COVID syndrome compared with no outpatient or inpatient contact. ['d7854e9bc9fe2098']
- Older age and female sex were associated with increased susceptibility to long-lasting COVID-19 symptoms. ['43ea8278ee20f0a4', '6d3f8e6ba0e5f08c']

title: Losartan and remote limb conditioning reduce brain edema in rodent models
summary: This community groups two rodent studies, one on losartan in NF2 schwannoma models and one on remote limb conditioning after stroke, both linked to brain edema. Both papers report a decrease in brain edema, and the claims show no conflicting directions. Each claim is worded as a direct causal relationship (strength 3), and press coverage of both was labelled aligned with the paper's strength. No retracted papers appear in this community.
key_findings:
- Losartan decreased neuro-edema and brain edema in NF2 mouse models. ['0bf80d72baddc90d']
- Remote limb conditioning after stroke decreased cerebral edema and brain swelling in mice. ['5ff60eba9af31447']

title: TFE3 overexpression and remote ischemic limb conditioning linked to motor function recovery
summary: This community groups two papers that share motor function as an outcome but study different exposures: TFE3 overexpression in an alpha-synuclein Parkinson's model and remote ischemic limb conditioning after stroke. Both papers state a direct causal increase in motor function, so the claims do not conflict. Press coverage matched only the stroke finding, which is labeled aligned with the paper, while the TFE3 finding has no press statement. Neither paper is retracted, and the claims do not address a shared mechanism.
key_findings:
- TFE3 overexpression reduces the loss of dopaminergic neurons and restores motor function in an alpha-synuclein overexpression model of Parkinson's disease. ['b20b9176817fcfdd']
- Remote ischemic limb conditioning after stroke shifts circulating monocytes to a CCR2+ proinflammatory subset and improves motor and gait function in chronic stroke. ['3cd5ea8960607ca1']
- Press coverage of the remote ischemic limb conditioning finding is aligned with its paper, while the TFE3 finding has no matched press statement. ['3cd5ea8960607ca1', 'b20b9176817fcfdd']
